source.title: I Grew Food on My Apartment Balcony for a Year (Here’s the Harvest)
source.transcript: Fourteen point six kilos of food from a four square metre balcony. That is what one year of growing on a rented balcony got me. Twelve months ago it looked like this, bare concrete and one sad plastic chair. The rules were simple: no yard, no landlord drama, nothing I could not carry up five floors. I started everything on the windowsill in yogurt cups...

key_frames.d: Close-up: a wicker basket of tomatoes, chard and herbs on a kitchen scale reading 14.6 kg. Bold white number on screen.
Wide shot of an empty grey concrete balcony, one plastic chair, overcast light. Text: 12 MONTHS EARLIER.
Top-down: rows of seedlings in labeled yogurt cups on a sunny windowsill. Hands with a spray bottle.
Handheld, shaky: young plants bending hard in the wind, creator ties stems to bamboo stakes.
A grey pigeon walks along the railing and pecks a strawberry. Creator laughs off-camera. Zoom-in meme cut.
Macro: tomatoes turning from green to red, golden-hour backlight.
Fast montage, one shot per month, a month label in the corner each time. Music swells.
Creator to camera beside a whiteboard listing harvest totals by crop.

comments.text: Mine faces north and gets maybe 3 hours of sun. Is it even worth trying??
How much did all of this cost in total? Would love a breakdown.
Please do a winter version! What happens after October?
The pigeon at 7:12 deserves its own video
Did the self-watering pots actually work while you were away?
Can I reuse the soil next year or do I need new?

analysis.summary: A renter turns an empty 4 m² concrete balcony into a food garden over twelve months and weighs every harvest.
analysis.hook: Opens on the final harvest on a kitchen scale (14.6 kg), then cuts back to the bare balcony twelve months earlier.
beats: Payoff first: the harvest on the scale
The empty balcony and the rules for the year
Moving outside and the wind problem
Totals and what to grow first
analysis.pacing: Cuts every 3 to 4 seconds in the first minute, then slows into a montage. Talking-head segments never run past 20 seconds.
why_it_worked: A hard number in the hook promises a payoff
Relatable limit: a rented balcony, no yard
Visible change over a fixed time span
A small recurring character (the pigeon) viewers remember

gaps.text: What grows with very little sun
Viewers with no balcony at all
One live-action look the whole way through

angles.title: Growing food on a balcony that gets 3 hours of sun
angles.pitch: The most-liked question in the comments: what actually grows when your balcony faces north.
angles.reason: Viewers with shady balconies were left without an answer. This is their obvious next click.
angles.suggested_title: Balcony Garden With Only 3 Hours of Sun: What Actually Grew
hooks: My balcony gets three hours of sun. Everyone said grow nothing. Here is what grew anyway.
Got a shady balcony? These five crops do not care.
I tracked every hour of light on a north-facing balcony for 90 days.
angles.hook_visual: narrow shaded balcony with a single band of sunlight crossing the planters

beats.t: First I measured the light. Three hours of direct sun, the rest bright shade.
beats.v: phone light meter held up on a narrow concrete balcony

beats.t: Leafy greens were the surprise. Lettuce, chard and spinach barely noticed.
beats.v: rows of lettuce and rainbow chard in long planters in soft shade

beats.t: Herbs split the room. Mint and parsley thrived, basil sulked.
beats.v: thriving mint beside a leggy, sad basil plant

beats.t: Tomatoes were the hard lesson. Plenty of leaves, four tomatoes total.
beats.v: tall tomato vine with only a few small green tomatoes

beats.t: If your balcony is shady, grow leaves, not fruit. Save this list for spring.
beats.v: overhead shot of a full basket of greens and herbs

beats.t: Lettuce bolts slower in shade, so my harvest window ran three extra weeks.
beats.v: calendar with three extra weeks circled beside lettuce

beats.t: Next time: a reflective panel on the back wall to bounce more light.
beats.v: white panel reflecting light onto planters

angles.title: What a year of balcony food actually cost
angles.pitch: Every receipt from the setup, set against the grocery value of what came out.
angles.reason: Cost was the second most common question. Same viewer, wants the numbers behind the harvest.
angles.suggested_title: I Added Up Every Cent of My Balcony Garden. Was It Worth It?
hooks: I spent $214 on a balcony garden. Here is exactly what it grew back.
Is growing food on a balcony actually cheaper? I kept every receipt.
Cost per tomato: $1.80. Cost per salad: 22 cents. Here is the math.
angles.hook_visual: a long receipt unrolling beside a basket of vegetables

beats.t: Setup was the big hit. Planters, soil and a drip kit came to $146.
beats.v: planters, soil bags and a drip kit with price tags

beats.t: Seeds were almost free. Eleven packets, $27, most still half full.
beats.v: grid of seed packets with small price labels

beats.t: Greens paid for themselves by month two.
beats.v: bar chart where grocery value crosses spend at month two

beats.t: Tomatoes and peppers never broke even on a balcony.
beats.v: a single tomato on a scale with a large price tag

beats.t: Year two costs a fraction of year one. The full spreadsheet is linked below.
beats.v: clean spreadsheet summary card with totals

beats.t: Water was the cost I forgot: about four dollars for the whole summer.
beats.v: watering can with a tiny coin stack

beats.t: Best value per square metre: salad greens, by a mile.
beats.v: ranking chart with salad greens at the top

angles.title: The winter balcony: growing through the cold months
angles.pitch: Picks up in October where the original stopped and follows the balcony through frost.
angles.reason: Continues the exact timeline of the reference video. Returning viewers want the next season.
angles.suggested_title: Balcony Garden in Winter: What Survives the Cold
hooks: The original year ended in October. This is what happened when I kept going.
Frost hit minus four. Six plants made it.
Everyone empties their balcony in winter. I tried the opposite.
angles.hook_visual: a snowy balcony railing with one green kale plant

beats.t: October: I swapped tomatoes for kale, garlic and winter lettuce.
beats.v: hands planting garlic cloves in a planter at dusk

beats.t: A cheap plastic cover bought me four degrees.
beats.v: a clear plastic cloche fogged with condensation over small plants

beats.t: The first frost took the lettuce, but the kale got sweeter.
beats.v: frost-covered kale leaves glittering in blue morning light

beats.t: By February the garlic was the only thing still pushing up.
beats.v: green garlic shoots through snow in a planter

beats.t: Winter will not feed you, but it keeps the balcony alive until spring.
beats.v: warm window light behind a snowy balcony garden

angles.title: The pigeon war
angles.pitch: The same balcony year retold as a rivalry with one very patient pigeon.
angles.reason: Same balcony, same viewers, new story. Comments show the pigeon moment was a favorite.
angles.suggested_title: Me vs. the Pigeons: A Balcony Garden Rivalry
hooks: They took my first strawberry. This meant war.
Twelve months, seven defenses, one very patient pigeon.
Every balcony gardener has an enemy. Mine has feathers.
angles.hook_visual: a cartoon pigeon holding a stolen strawberry

beats.t: Week one. A pigeon named Gus inspects the new planters.
beats.v: cartoon pigeon peering over a planter rim

beats.t: Defense one: a fake owl. Gus sat on it.
beats.v: cartoon pigeon sitting smugly on a plastic owl

beats.t: Defense two: netting. Gus found the gap in an hour.
beats.v: pigeon squeezing through a gap in green netting

beats.t: What finally worked: shiny tape and a pot of seeds just for him.
beats.v: reflective ribbons fluttering while a pigeon eats from its own pot

beats.t: Truce. Gus gets one pot. I get the strawberries.
beats.v: pigeon and gardener sharing the balcony at sunset

angles.title: A year on the balcony, told by the tomato plant
angles.pitch: The reference video’s exact timeline, narrated by the plant that lived it.
angles.reason: Same beats as the reference video from a new point of view, so its viewers recognize every moment.
angles.suggested_title: My Balcony Garden Year, From the Tomato’s Point of View
hooks: Hi. I am the tomato. Nobody asked me how this year went.
Day one I was a seed in a yogurt cup. Let me tell you what happened next.
You watched her grow me. Here is my side of the story.
angles.hook_visual: a cartoon tomato plant with a face standing in a pot on a balcony

beats.t: They kept me in a yogurt cup on the windowsill for six weeks.
beats.v: small tomato seedling in a yogurt cup on a sunny windowsill

beats.t: Then the move outside. The wind up here is no joke.
beats.v: young tomato plant bending in the wind on a high balcony

beats.t: July was glorious. I put out forty flowers.
beats.v: tomato plant covered in yellow flowers in bright sun

beats.t: Then the pigeon came for my fruit. We do not speak of it.
beats.v: tomato plant glaring at a pigeon on the railing

beats.t: Eleven tomatoes. Proud. Save my seeds for next year.
beats.v: tomato plant beside a bowl of ripe red tomatoes

angles.title: No balcony at all: a windowsill food garden
angles.pitch: The same goal, scaled down to a single 40 cm windowsill.
angles.reason: Reaches renters in the same audience who could not follow the original because they have no balcony.
angles.suggested_title: No Balcony? I Grew Food on One Windowsill for 6 Months
hooks: No balcony. No yard. One windowsill. Six months of food.
If you do not have a balcony, this one is for you.
Forty centimetres of windowsill grew more than I expected.
angles.hook_visual: one crowded windowsill of plants seen from inside a small apartment

beats.t: The rule: everything had to fit on one sill, forty centimetres wide.
beats.v: a narrow windowsill with a tape measure across it

beats.t: Microgreens were ready in nine days.
beats.v: dense tray of microgreens in morning light

beats.t: Green onions regrew from grocery scraps, again and again.
beats.v: green onion roots in a glass of water

beats.t: A dwarf chili gave me sixty peppers.
beats.v: small chili plant covered in red peppers

beats.t: Start with microgreens this week. The full list is below.
beats.v: hands snipping microgreens over a plate

angles.title: Vacation-proof: testing self-watering pots for 14 days
angles.pitch: Three watering setups, two weeks away, one heatwave.
angles.reason: Answers a direct question about a product that appears briefly in the reference video.
angles.suggested_title: I Left My Balcony Garden Alone for 14 Days. Did Self-Watering Pots Work?
hooks: I left for two weeks and told nobody to water my plants.
Three watering systems, fourteen days, one heatwave.
Do self-watering pots really work? I tested them the hard way.
angles.hook_visual: a suitcase by the door with balcony plants behind

beats.t: Three setups: wicking pots, a drip timer, and plain pots as a control.
beats.v: three labeled planters side by side

beats.t: Day four, a heatwave hit 34 degrees.
beats.v: thermometer reading 34 degrees over a sunny balcony

beats.t: Plain pots were crisp by day six.
beats.v: wilted plant in a dry terracotta pot

beats.t: Wicking pots held on. The drip timer won outright.
beats.v: comparison chart with the drip timer ahead

beats.t: For a long trip, pair a wicking pot with a drip line.
beats.v: diagram of a drip line feeding a wicking pot

angles.title: Who pollinates a fifth-floor garden?
angles.pitch: Thirty days of camera footage on the flower boxes to see who shows up.
angles.reason: Same niche and viewers with a new topic. Fewer shared keywords lowers the score.
angles.suggested_title: Do Bees Reach a 5th-Floor Balcony? I Counted.
hooks: My tomatoes flowered but nothing set. So I started counting visitors.
Five floors up, who is actually pollinating your plants?
I filmed my balcony flowers for 30 days to see who showed up.
angles.hook_visual: one bee flying above a city skyline toward a balcony flower

beats.t: Thirty days of footage on the flower boxes.
beats.v: small camera clipped to a balcony railing pointed at flowers

beats.t: Bees came, but only on warm, still mornings.
beats.v: bee on a yellow tomato flower in morning light

beats.t: Hoverflies did more work than I expected.
beats.v: hoverfly above white flowers, shallow focus

beats.t: On windy weeks I pollinated by hand with a toothbrush.
beats.v: electric toothbrush touching a tomato flower stem

beats.t: Plant flowers next to your vegetables. Here is what drew the most visitors.
beats.v: box of mixed flowers next to vegetable planters

angles.title: The same year, painted as a watercolor timelapse
angles.pitch: The balcony year again, told through one painting a week.
angles.reason: Same story as the reference video with a new visual treatment, so the same audience recognizes it.
angles.suggested_title: A Year of Balcony Gardening, Painted Week by Week
hooks: I painted my balcony garden every week for a year.
Fifty-two paintings. One balcony. Watch it grow.
This is a year of growing food, one watercolor at a time.
angles.hook_visual: watercolor of a balcony garden being painted in fast strokes

beats.t: January: bare pots and a sketch of a plan.
beats.v: watercolor of empty pots and a pencil garden plan

beats.t: April: the first seedlings, and the color comes back.
beats.v: watercolor of seedlings in bright green washes

beats.t: July: the page gets crowded.
beats.v: dense watercolor of an overflowing summer balcony

beats.t: October: the harvest, in reds and golds.
beats.v: watercolor of a harvest basket in warm reds and gold

beats.t: The full sketchbook flip is at the end.
beats.v: a watercolor sketchbook flipping through pages

angles.title: Reusing last year’s soil: what happens
angles.pitch: Old soil against new soil, side by side, for one season.
angles.reason: A direct follow-up for viewers who started a garden after the reference video and are now in year two.
angles.suggested_title: Can You Reuse Potting Soil? My Year-Two Balcony Test
hooks: I could buy new soil or reuse last year’s. So I did both.
Year two. Same soil. Did it still grow anything?
Old soil versus new soil, side by side, one season.
angles.hook_visual: a scoop of old potting soil held over a planter

beats.t: Half the planters got fresh soil. Half got last year’s.
beats.v: two planters, one dark fresh soil and one pale old soil

beats.t: Old soil, untreated, grew pale and slow.
beats.v: pale yellowish lettuce seedlings in old soil

beats.t: Old soil plus compost and worm castings caught up in three weeks.
beats.v: hands mixing compost into a planter

beats.t: By harvest you could not tell them apart.
beats.v: two equally lush planters side by side

beats.t: Reuse your soil. Just feed it first. My mix is below.
beats.v: flat lay of compost, worm castings and a scoop
